paragraphs.heading: A pulsar with a partner
paragraphs.text: A binary pulsar is a pulsar that orbits together with a partner star. That partner is often a white dwarf or a neutron star, and in the double pulsar PSR J0737-3039 the partner is a second pulsar. The partner is usually hard or even impossible to see. Astronomers still know it is there, because radio telescopes can time the pulses with great accuracy, and the timing gives the partner away.

paragraphs.heading: Why physicists care
paragraphs.text: The gravity around a binary pulsar is very strong. That makes these systems one of the few places where physicists can put general relativity to the test. Studying one of them also gave the first accurate measurement of how heavy neutron stars are, using timing effects that come from relativity.

paragraphs.heading: The Hulse-Taylor discovery
paragraphs.text: The pulsar PSR B1913+16, often called the Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar, was found at Arecibo in 1974 by Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor. Hulse noticed that its pulse rate sped up and slowed down in a regular pattern. The explanation was that the pulsar was racing around another star in a tight orbit. When it moved toward Earth the pulses arrived more often, and when it moved away they arrived less often; this is the Doppler effect. From these changes the pair worked out that the two stars weigh about the same, so the partner was likely a neutron star too. The work won them the 1993 Nobel Prize in Physics.

paragraphs.heading: A clock in orbit
paragraphs.text: The pulses behave like the ticks of a clock, and changes in the ticking show changes in the pulsar's speed toward or away from us. Relativity also tugs on this clock. When the two stars are close, gravity is stronger, time passes more slowly, and the gap between ticks grows; in the weakest part of the field the clock wins that time back. A second effect from special relativity, called time dilation, works around the orbit in a similar way. Today the pulses from this system are timed to within 15 μs.

paragraphs.heading: A shrinking orbit
paragraphs.text: Relativity predicts that two bodies in orbit slowly turn their orbital energy into gravitational radiation. Taylor, Joel Weisberg and colleagues checked this by measuring the orbital period of PSR B1913+16. From 1982 on, they reported that the closest approach of the two stars did not match what an unchanging orbit would give. In the ten years after the discovery, the orbital period fell by about 76 millionths of a second each year, so the pulsar reached its farthest point more than a second early. This decay matched Einstein's equations almost perfectly, and later observations keep showing it.

paragraphs.heading: When the partner spills over
paragraphs.text: Sometimes the partner is a fairly normal star that grows so large that it spills past its Roche lobe, pouring its outer layers onto the pulsar. The gas heats up as it crosses over and can give off X-rays that seem to pulse, a phase called the X-ray binary stage. The flowing matter often builds a disk around the star that receives it, called an accretion disk. Pulsars also blow out a wind of particles moving at close to light speed, which can strip away the partner's magnetosphere and change the pulses a great deal.
